title: Ang 411–431: Asa ashtpadis
hookLine: longer hymns, including Nanak's lament for Saidpur on ang 417
tomorrow: what did a boy write on his school slate?

lines: A WEDDING NEXT TO A WAR.
BRAIDS, AND RED IN THE PARTING.
cards: Scroll long enough and a feed will put a wedding video right next to the news from a war. On ang 417, Guru Nanak puts them together on purpose, and it's strange.
In a lament for a town overrun, which tradition names as Saidpur, he doesn't count the dead. He describes hair. Braids.
A line of red in the parting. Grooms who looked so fine beside their brides. Why?
For parents: this hymn mourns the aftermath of an attack, without graphic detail.

teach.h: BRAIDS, AND RED IN THE PARTING.
teach.b: From ang 411, Guru Nanak's Asa hymns grow longer: the ashtpadis. On ang 417, in paraphrase: those heads that shone with braids, with red in the parting, are shorn now, and dust is in their throats.
They lived in fine houses; now they can't even sit near. When they were married, their grooms looked handsome beside them, and they came home in palanquins. Now there are ropes at their necks.
The puzzle answers itself. Numbers numb us. A wedding doesn't.

teach.h: MEASURE THE LOSS BY THE JOY.
teach.b: Guru Nanak measures the loss by the joy it took: hair someone braided that morning, the ride to a new home. Nobody can scroll past that. And notice who he grieves.
These are the wealthy, the women from the fine houses. He doesn't say they had it coming.
Then, in paraphrase, he says their wealth and beauty, which had brought them such delight, became their enemies, and he turns, as on ang 360, to the One who gives and takes.
A lament in scripture makes room for anyone grieving: stop, look, name each loss, and give it a melody.

how: Guru Nanak's Asa ashtpadis, including the lament on ang 417, are read in order and sung as kirtan; Sikhs remember these hymns as the Guru grieving with ordinary people in a time of invasion.

p: braids and red in the parting

s: the lament on ang 417 counts the dead
it describes braids, red in the parting, grooms and palanquins: the joy that was lost.
Guru Nanak grieves even for the wealthy in this hymn
the women from the fine houses; he grieves them as people.
faith means skipping past grief quickly
this lament stops, names each loss, and sings it, in scripture.

games.q: a friend's dog has died, and she's posting old photos all day. someone tells her 'just stop looking at them.' what fits ang 417?
o: let her look; naming each small detail is how a lament grieves.
agree: the past is gone, so photos only keep the pain alive.
send her a funny video to change the subject for her.
games.why: Guru Nanak measures loss by the small joys it took, braid by braid, and gives it a melody instead of hurrying past.

practice: Read ang 417 slowly if you can, even a few lines. Then close your eyes and let one loss come to mind, yours or someone else's, near or far. Don't fix it or explain it.
Hold one small detail of it, the way the hymn holds a braid, and stay with it gently.
